notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Job 37, drawn from the sources I was able to retrieve and read.

---

## Job 37 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview (Introduction)

Elihu's fourth and final speech. He calls Job and the others to look at a gathering thunderstorm and see in it the majesty, power, and unsearchable wisdom of God. The chapter functions as a bridge to the Lord's own speech from the whirlwind (ch. 38). Elihu's descriptions of weather phenomena are noted by scholars — including Alexander von Humboldt — as remarkably acute observational writing for the ancient world. (Ellicott calls it "one of the fine passages of the book.")

Dr. Constable notes that Elihu may be describing autumn conditions in 36:27–33, winter in 37:1–13, and summer in 37:17–18. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-37.html)

Gill summarises the chapter structure: thunder and lightning (vv. 1–5); snow, rain, wind and frost (vv. 6–13); then an application to Job to consider these wonders and humbly fear God (vv. 14–24). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 1 — “At this my heart also pounds and leaps from its place.”

Elihu is speaking of a thunderstorm gathering. His own heart trembles — not only are cattle terrified (as at the end of ch. 36), but even the speaker himself shakes. Gill says that such is the terrible majesty of God that all rational creatures, even devils, tremble. He speculates that a literal storm was rising at that moment, since soon after, God speaks from the whirlwind (Job 38:1). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

Ellicott agrees: "Not only are the cattle terrified, but at this also my heart trembleth and is moved out of its place." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 2 — “Listen closely to the thunder of His voice and the rumbling that comes from His mouth.”

Elihu urges attentive listening. Thunder is uniquely suited as a metaphor for God's voice — only thunder befits the majesty of the Almighty, an insight David Guzik (Enduring Word) draws from Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

Gill notes the distinction: "the noise of his voice" refers to the loud thunderclap, while "the sound that goeth out of his mouth" may refer to the lower, rumbling noise before the cloud bursts. He adds that the voice of God — whether in nature, providence, law or Gospel — is always to be hearkened to attentively. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 3 — “He unleashes His lightning beneath the whole sky and sends it to the ends of the earth.”

Gill: God "directs" the thunder and lightning — nothing is by chance. Where the lightning strikes, which tree, house or person, is under His direction. He also sees an emblem of the Gospel: as lightning flashes from east to west, so the light of the Gospel spread from the east to all nations before Jerusalem's fall. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

Ellicott: "He directeth it" means He sendeth it forth — the noise and rumbling which fills all heaven, and the lightning to the earth's ends. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 4 — “Then there comes a roaring sound; He thunders with His majestic voice. He does not restrain the lightning when His voice resounds.”

Ellicott explains that the thunderclap follows the lightning flash. The difficult phrase "he will not stay them" he interprets as: "Yet none can track them (the thunder and lightning) when His voice is heard. They travel in paths which none can explore." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

Gill notes an alternative: God "will not supplant or deceive" — when He thunders, He does not act as a subtle enemy but openly as King. Or simply: the rain and hail are not stayed; they follow after the thunder. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 5 — “God thunders wondrously with His voice; He does great things we cannot comprehend.”

Elihu's recurring theme: God's works are beyond human comprehension. David Guzik notes that Elihu is "partially correct" — Job had indeed presumed to know more than he could or should. But Elihu wrongly assumed Job's crisis came from his sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

Gill adds that the thunder produces marvellous effects: rending rocks, shattering oaks and cedars (as in Psalm 29). He sees the Gospel's effects as analogous — quickening dead sinners, casting down strongholds of sin and Satan. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 6 — “For He says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and to the gentle rain, ‘Pour out a mighty downpour.’”

All operations of nature obey God's command. Gill observes that in the original Hebrew the phrase to the snow is literally "Be thou earth" (a defective spelling noted by Aben Ezra), meaning "be on the earth." He comments on the wonders of snow — how it falls in hot countries like parts of Africa, yet also lies continually on the summit of burning Mount Etna. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

Ellicott: "All the operations of nature obey the behest of God — the snow, the gentle showers, the drenching downpour." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 7 — “He seals up the hand of every man, so that all men may know His work.”

When God sends snow, cold, and heavy rain, outdoor labour becomes impossible. The farmer's hand is "sealed" — he cannot work. David Guzik, citing Spurgeon: "When the Lord seals up a man's hand, he is unable to perform his labor. The Lord has an object in this, namely, 'that all men may know his work.' When they cannot do their own work, they are intended to observe the works of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

Gill: men are stopped so they may have leisure to reflect on their moral ways, and to know and own that the snow and rain are God's work. Some read it: "that all men of His work may know" — i.e., all men, whom He has made, may know Him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

Ellicott: "Men may learn from these things that they and their works are under the control of God. They are not the entirely free agents they suppose." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 8 — “The wild animals enter their lairs; they settle down in their dens.”

Not only man but beasts also are affected. When snow and rain abound, wild beasts cannot prowl; they retreat to dens. Gill draws a parallel: as great personages, comparable to beasts of prey for savageness, will flee to rocks and caves to hide in the day of God's wrath (Revelation 6:15). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

Ellicott: "And not man only, but the beasts likewise, have to take refuge in their dens and coverts." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 9 — “The tempest comes from its chamber, and the cold from the driving north winds.”

Ellicott says the Hebrew is better rendered: "Out of its chamber (see Job 9:9) cometh the whirlwind, or typhoon: and cold from the northern constellations, from the quarter of the heavens where they shine." The "chamber" is a reference to the hidden storehouses or treasuries of God. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

Gill notes that the Hebrew for "north" can also mean "the scatterers" — referring to northern winds that scatter clouds, drive away rain, and bring fair weather. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 10 — “By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen.”

"By the breath of God" means by His command or word — or, as Gill notes, a freezing north wind described as the breath of His nostrils (cf. Psalm 18:15). The "breadth of the waters is straitened" means the waters are bound up, reduced in compass, made firm as a molten mass. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

Ellicott: "The breadth of the waters is straitened — firm, like a molten mass." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 11 — “He loads the clouds with moisture; He scatters His lightning through them.”

Gill: God "wearieth the thick cloud" by filling it with so much water that it is like a weary traveller — and then empties it, so the cloud spends itself. An emblem of ministers who "spend and are spent" for the good of men. "He scattereth his bright cloud" — thin, light clouds soon dispersed; an emblem of clouds without water (Jude 12) or of sins forgiven and scattered (Isaiah 44:22). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

Ellicott: "Also He ladeth the thick cloud with moisture, maketh it to be charged with rain. He scattereth the cloud of His lightning, i.e., which containeth His lightning." He also notes an alternative rendering where the sun is the subject: "Yea, the bright sun weareth out (disperseth) the thick cloud." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 12 — “They swirl about, whirling at His direction, accomplishing all that He commands over the face of all the earth.”

The clouds are "turned round about by His counsels" — God sits at the helm (as Gill notes the Hebrew imagery) and steers them. David Guzik: "God's creation swirls and submits to His guidance perfectly, and Elihu means to imply that Job should do the same." He adds that the storm serves as a metaphor for apparent chaos under absolute divine control. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

---

### v. 13 — “Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion.”

The three purposes of the storm: (1) for correction (chastisement of men for sin); (2) for His land (to water and make it fruitful); (3) for mercy (to do good, to show lovingkindness). Gill notes that the same rain cloud may be sent in judgment on one place and in mercy on another. He also points out the Hebrew word rendered "loving devotion" (chesed) is the word for mercy or covenant faithfulness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

W.F. Adeney (Pulpit Commentary) expands: "What looks like a calamity may be a blessing. Instead of complaining of the inconvenience of what happens to us, let us look round us and see if it is bringing good in some other direction. … The scourge is a blessing in disguise." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 14 — “Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the wonders of God.”

Elihu addresses Job directly and personally — more so than the three friends. David Guzik: "Young Elihu again appealed to Job in a very direct and personal way." Matthew Poole is quoted: "If there be so much matter of wonder and adoration in the most obvious and sensible works of God, how wonderful must his deep and secret counsels and judgments be!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

R. Green (Pulpit Commentary) says Elihu would teach Job "to hearken to the Lord rather than reply to him, to learn rather than teach." The works of God are a revelation of divine greatness, divine goodness, and the hidden purpose of God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/37.htm)

W.F. Adeney elaborates the threefold response: (1) with attention — "hearken"; (2) with patience — "stand still"; (3) with thought — "consider." He observes: "We talk too much about the works of God; it would be better if we would be silent and let them speak to us." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 15 — “Do you know how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash?”

The series of rhetorical questions begins — the same kind God Himself will use in chapters 38–41. Ellicott: "Dost thou know all the secrets of God's thunderbolts, at whom and how He will use them?" He notes an alternative reading: "Dost thou know when God setteth the sun over them (the clouds), and causeth the light (i.e., the sun) to shine upon His cloud?" — i.e., how God uses the sun to disperse the clouds. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

David Guzik: "Significantly, God will address Job among similar lines when God begins to speak starting at Job 38 (Do you know… Do you know)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

---

### v. 16 — “Do you understand how the clouds float, those wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge?”

The "balancings of the clouds" — how they are poised and suspended in the sky — is a wonder. Ellicott quotes Coleridge: "Ye clouds, that far above me float and pause." God is "perfect in knowledge" — the One who orchestrates these marvels knows all things perfectly, a striking contrast to Job's limited understanding. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 17 — “You whose clothes get hot when the land lies hushed under the south wind…”

Elihu points to Job's everyday experience: when the south wind blows and the land is still and stifling, Job's garments grow hot against his skin. The point: Job cannot explain even this simple phenomenon, let alone the deep purposes of providence. Ellicott renders: "When he quieteth the earth — or, When the earth is still." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 18 — “Can you, like Him, spread out the skies to reflect the heat like a mirror of bronze?”

Elihu asks whether Job helped God spread out the sky. In the ancient Near East, polished metal mirrors (often bronze) gave a reflection. The image is of a sky made hard and reflective like burnished metal under the glaring sun. Ellicott says some understand this of the sun dispersing clouds, but more probably it refers to God spreading out the magnificent dome of heaven — though the wording implies the clouds rather than a cloudless sky. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 19 — “Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case when our faces are in darkness.”

Elihu's irony: "Job, since you insist God owes you an audience, please teach us what to say to Him." David Guzik: "Here, Elihu confronted what he believed to be Job's arrogance in saying that man deserved an audience or a justification from God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

Ellicott proposes a different interpretation — that "him" refers to the sun, not God directly: "He is altogether hidden by the clouds; but is he gone? is he not still there behind them?" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

W.F. Adeney (Pulpit) draws a parallel to the disciples' request in Luke 11:1 — "Teach us to pray." Both Elihu and the disciples felt their inability to speak rightly to God "by reason of darkness" (ignorance and sin). He says: "The confession of our inability to pray is the first step towards doing so acceptably." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 20 — “Should He be told that I want to speak? Would a man ask to be swallowed up?”

Elihu's point: to demand speech with God is to court destruction. "If a man speak, surely he shall be swallowed up." Ellicott says if understood of the sun, the sense is: "Shall it be told of him? … hath any man ever ventured to say, in such a case, that the sun is swallowed up, extinguished?" — i.e., no one would dare declare the sun has perished when it is merely hidden behind clouds. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 21 — “Now no one can gaze at the sun when it is bright in the skies after the wind has swept them clean.”

The brilliance of the sun when clouds are cleared is unbearable to human eyes. Ellicott interprets "the bright light" as the sun: "But he is bright behind the clouds, and when the wind has passed over them and cleared them away, even the north wind, he will come forth like gold; but upon God there is terrible majesty." He calls this rendering "great sublimity" and says it points forward to the opening of the next chapter. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

W.F. Adeney expands: "God veils his glory in clouds… His unveiled glory would be an unbearable light." This is so because (1) ignorance is dazzled by absolute knowledge, (2) sin shrinks from perfect holiness, and (3) finite life cannot endure the fulness of infinite life. God educates us by gradually unveiling His glory. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 22 — “Out of the north He comes in golden splendour; awesome majesty surrounds Him.”

"Fair weather cometh out of the north" (KJV) — or, as the BSB renders, "Out of the north He comes in golden splendour." The north wind clears the clouds, and golden light breaks forth. This is an image of God Himself: He comes in golden splendour, surrounded by terrible majesty. David Guzik (quoting Bullinger): "Just as when a storm has dispersed all the dark clouds and cleared the air, so, when God reveals Himself, His light and truth are seen." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

---

### v. 23 — “The Almighty is beyond our reach; He is exalted in power! In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress.”

Elihu's great summary of God's character. Gill picks up four points: (1) "we cannot find Him out" — He is unsearchable; (2) "excellent in power" — displayed in creation, redemption, and providence; (3) "in judgment" — His righteous government of the world; (4) "in plenty of justice" — He is most just, and His great power does not lead Him to abuse it. Gill also notes the rendering "he will not afflict" may be read as "he will not answer" — i.e., He does not give account of His dealings. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

David Guzik notes the deep irony: "The God whom Elihu believed to be utterly beyond and unreachable by man (we cannot find Him) has come in the storm, and will speak to Job." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

W.F. Adeney: "We can trust God for what he is, even when we do not understand what he does. … Because we believe in the equity of God, we must expect him to act in mystery." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/37.htm)

---

### v. 24 — “Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart.”

The chapter's conclusion: men should fear (reverence) God. He shows no partiality to those who are "wise of heart" — i.e., wise in their own eyes. Ellicott notes a wordplay in the Hebrew between *yĕre'u* (they shall fear) and *yireh* (he shall see): "Therefore men may fear Him; but as for the wise in heart, no one even of them shall see Him." He says this is probably the intended meaning, since the literal KJV rendering implies God does not regard the truly wise, which is a "doubtful sentiment." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/37.htm)

Gill: men should fear God because of His greatness in power, judgment, and justice, and because of His goodness in not afflicting for His pleasure's sake. The "wise of heart" here are those wise in their own conceit. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/37.htm)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds that "the Lord majestic respects none who is wise of heart, in his own conceit, who acts moronic saying, 'there is no God,' or acting as if none existed" (cf. Psalm 14:1; Romans 12:16; 1 Corinthians 3:18–20). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-37.html)

Grant's Commentary: "Whether Job or his friends, all of whom considered themselves wise, their wisdom did not impress God, and he showed no partiality to any of them, as they may have hoped He would." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-37.html)

---

## Protestant Traditions — Where They Differ

On this particular chapter, the consulted sources show **broad agreement across Protestant traditions** rather than sharp disagreement. The chapter is largely descriptive nature poetry applied to the doctrine of God's majesty. However, some distinct emphases emerge:

### Reformed / Calvin
Calvin's commentary on Job 37 is available at BibleHub but could not be fetched within limits. However, his general approach (seen in the preceptaustin.org summaries of Elihu's speeches) emphasises God's absolute sovereignty over nature and providence — that the storm's apparent chaos is under God's total control, and that God's hiddenness does not compromise His justice. The Reformed tradition tends to read Elihu's speeches as genuinely preparatory for God's theophany, not as yet another misguided human speech.

### Baptist (Spurgeon / Gill)
Spurgeon (cited in Enduring Word on v. 7) draws practical application: God stops men's ordinary work so they may observe His. Gill consistently finds typological meanings — e.g., the lightning spreading to the ends of the earth as a type of the Gospel's spread. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary reads v. 24 as a warning against practical atheism.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik emphasises the experiential presence of God in the storm and the dramatic irony that the "unreachable" God is about to speak. His reading tends to be more narrative-driven — highlighting the drama and the personal encounter with God that follows in ch. 38. He is also more critical of Elihu than some traditions: Elihu is "young, brash, and almost right" — his premise (that Job's crisis comes from sin) is wrong, even though many of his statements about God are correct. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-37/)

### Anglican / Ellicott
Ellicott brings philological expertise, especially on the Hebrew text. He is distinctive in suggesting that vv. 19–21 may be speaking of the *sun* rather than God directly — an interpretation not found in most other sources consulted. This reading sees the sun as a type: hidden behind clouds but certain to emerge, pointing to God's hidden-but-certain majesty.

### Methodist / Wesleyan
The Pulpit Commentary homiletics by W.F. Adeney (a broadly Protestant source used across traditions) focus on devotional application: "The Prayer for Prayer" (v. 19), "Unbearable Light" (v. 21), "The Mystery of God" (v. 23). The emphasis falls on reverent submission, patient trust, and God's educative purposes in suffering.

### Lutheran
No distinctively Lutheran source on this chapter was retrievable within limits. Lutheran commentaries generally align with the historic Protestant reading of Elihu as preparing the way for God's speech, emphasising the theology of the cross — that God hides Himself under suffering and apparent absence, yet remains sovereign and good.

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes)
Could not be fetched within limits. NET Bible notes generally provide textual and translational detail — e.g., on the Hebrew wordplay in v. 24 between "fear" and "see," and on the alternative rendering of "chamber" in v. 9 as the storehouses of the heavens.

### Critical Scholarship on Elihu's Speeches
Dr. Constable notes that some critical scholars believe chapters 32–37 were inserted by a later editor, though many conservatives affirm their authenticity. Larry J. Waters is cited defending the authenticity of Elihu's speeches. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-37.html)

### Catholic and Orthodox
No distinct Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter was retrievable within search/fetch limits. The Catholic tradition (e.g., the *New Advent* / *Catholic Encyclopedia* approach) generally follows the same broad reading, often drawing on the Church Fathers and Thomas Aquinas's *Literal Exposition on Job*, which sees Elihu as speaking truth about God's majesty but missing the mystery of innocent suffering.

---

*Sources consulted: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Gill's Exposition, Ellicott's Commentary for English Readers, Pulpit Commentary Homiletics (Adeney & Green), Dr. Constable's Expository Notes, Grant's Commentary, Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, Matthew Henry (via excerpts), Lange's Commentary (via excerpts), Expositor's Bible Commentary (via excerpts), and Precept Austin (summary notes).*
